mechanism_description: A venom peptide of a small rattlesnake that binds the fibrinogen-binding site of one human platelet surface receptor (an integrin) and so stops platelets sticking together. A seven-residue ring copying the peptide's binding loop has the same action. Secreted, one gene, no cofactor.

A small protein that a cold-water fish secretes into its own body fluids, where it binds the surface of ice crystals and stops them growing. Added to a storage solution it let rat hearts be kept below zero for 24 hours. One gene, one small domain, works alone, but what it binds is ice rather than a protein.

A small protein secreted by a blood-feeding worm into its host, which blocks the first step of human clotting by holding a two-protein starter complex inactive. One gene, small single domain, no cofactor; it binds a complex rather than a single protein.

A short designed peptide: a human hormone peptide with the tail of a snake venom peptide stuck on the end. It switches on two human receptor enzymes at the cell surface. Small, secreted, no cofactor; only part of it comes from the animal.

A disordered protein from the cytoplasm of a tardigrade that forms a gel as it dries and holds other proteins in shape. In a vial it keeps a human clotting protein working through drying and heat. One gene, one chain, but it acts as a bulk protectant rather than by binding a site, and it works inside the organism's own cells.

An enzyme purified from ram testes, in two sugar-decorated forms of the same protein, that cuts the hyaluronan chains between human cells. Secreted, one catalytic chain, no cofactor; the sugar groups are part of the molecule.

A blood protein of a snake-eating marsupial, circulating in its own plasma, that binds and switches off venom enzymes. It is secreted, binds a target, and comes from a single gene family, but several different proteins act together in the animal and each one blocks a different venom component.

A small molecule, not a protein, copying part of a large chemical made by a marine sponge. It binds tubulin inside human cells and stops microtubules growing. It is made by a multi-enzyme pathway in the animal, so no single gene carries it, but the molecule itself acts alone on one conserved target.

A peptide copying the two thrombin-contacting ends of a protein in the saliva of a blood-feeding leech. It is secreted into the host's blood and blocks one human clotting enzyme, thrombin, by binding both its active site and its substrate groove. Twenty residues, one chain, no partner needed.

A venom toxin of a rattlesnake made of two different subunits that must stay together: a membrane-cutting enzyme and a chaperone subunit that aims it. Secreted, catalytic, but it needs its partner subunit and calcium, and its effect is on cell membranes broadly.

A small disulfide-bonded peptide from the venom of a sea anemone, released outside the animal, that blocks one human potassium channel on the surface of a subset of T cells. About 35 residues, a single folded domain, no cofactor and no partner protein.

A small disulfide-bonded peptide copied from one that pig white blood cells use to kill microbes. It is stored as a precursor inside the cell and cut to the active form. It punches holes in microbial membranes, so its target is not a protein humans share.

A lipid-and-protein extract of pig lung, acting at the air-liquid surface of the lung. Almost all of it is lipid; the small proteins only help the film spread. The action is physical surface tension lowering, needs the lipids, and is not one gene's product.

A secreted protein that regenerating nerves switch on in a salamander's limb stump, released from gland cells under the wound skin, and enough on its own to let a nerve-cut stump regrow digits. One gene and secreted, but it only works inside a limb stump that already has the right cells and nerve signals.

A mixture of single-stranded DNA fragments, 14-19 kDa on average, extracted from pig gut tissue. It acts on the lining cells of blood vessels from the outside; no one receptor is named for it. It is not the product of a single gene, and its effect is on a cell layer rather than on one binding partner.

The whole salivary anticoagulant protein of a blood-feeding leech, made in bacteria: a single 65-residue secreted chain that binds one human clotting enzyme, thrombin, and holds it inactive. One gene, no cofactor, no partner.
A snake venom enzyme that cuts one end off human fibrinogen, stripping clotting protein out of the blood. It is secreted, catalytic, a single chain of moderate size, and needs no cofactor.
A 13-residue piece of a peptide found in the paralytic saliva of a shrew. It blocks one human calcium channel that many tumours carry a lot of. One gene, secreted, very small, works alone.

A burrowing rodent survives 18 minutes with no oxygen by running its energy metabolism on fructose instead of glucose, using a sugar transporter and a sugar kinase expressed throughout its tissues. This is a whole metabolic route inside cells, needing several proteins and the right substrate, not one molecule that could be handed over.

A short positively charged peptide from frog skin secretion, about 22 residues in the version used, which kills bacteria by breaking their membranes. One gene, secreted, small, no cofactor; what it acts on is a microbial membrane, not a protein that humans and other animals share.

A mixture of digestive enzymes extracted from pig pancreas. The enzymes are secreted ones and each is catalytic, but the product is many gene products together, and what they act on is food in the gut rather than a human protein.

A shortened version of a 39-residue peptide from the oral secretion of a venomous lizard, missing its first eight residues. It sits on the same human gut-hormone receptor as the full peptide but blocks it instead of switching it on. One gene, small, secreted, no partner needed.

A 25-residue disulfide-bonded peptide from the venom of a fish-hunting marine snail, injected into prey. It blocks the pore of one human voltage-gated calcium channel in nerve endings. One gene, one small folded chain, works on its own.

An enzyme purified from bull testes that cuts the hyaluronan chains of the jelly between human cells, so fluid moves more freely through the tissue. It is secreted, acts outside cells, is a single catalytic protein, and needs no cofactor.
A snake venom enzyme that cuts human fibrinogen into fibrin, used to strip clotting protein from the blood. Secreted, catalytic, a single chain, no cofactor.

Cow haemoglobin taken out of red cells and chemically cross-linked, infused to carry oxygen in plasma. It is a large four-chain protein with a haem iron group, works inside the circulation rather than on a receptor, and needs its haem cofactor and its multi-chain assembly.

A bear lies still for months and loses no bone. Bone turnover stays balanced and suppressed, and the measurements point to hormone signalling that the animal shares with humans, with no animal-specific molecule identified. The effect is a whole-body state, not a molecule that can be moved.

A lipid-and-protein extract of calf lung, acting at the air-liquid surface of the lung. Two small hydrophobic proteins work together with the lipids to spread a film and lower surface tension. The effect is physical, needs the lipid partners, and comes from more than one gene.
A 32-residue hormone that a fish secretes into its own blood to control calcium. It binds the matching human cell-surface receptor on bone cells. One gene, one small secreted chain, no cofactor.

A nuclear protein of a tardigrade that sits on nucleosomes and protects the DNA wrapped on them from hydroxyl radicals. One gene, one chain, and it binds a structure conserved across animals, but it works inside the nucleus and must be expressed in the cell to do anything.

An enzyme in the saliva of a blood-feeding bat that switches on the human clot-dissolving protein plasminogen, and only does so where fibrin is present. Secreted, catalytic, one gene; it acts through a human partner protein, so it needs that protein to be there.

A short peptide found in the venom of a pit viper, secreted into another animal's bloodstream, that blocks a single human blood-pressure enzyme (angiotensin-converting enzyme) at its active site. A small synthetic molecule copying the peptide's contact points does the same. One gene makes the peptide; it needs no partner protein and no cofactor.

A short, strongly positive arginine-rich peptide from fish sperm nuclei, where its normal job is packing DNA. In blood it works by sticking to a negatively charged sugar chain and cancelling it. One gene, small peptide, no cofactor, but its action is charge binding rather than catalysis on a protein target.

A shortened form of a zinc-dependent enzyme from snake venom that cuts the fibrin of a human clot directly. Secreted, catalytic, one chain; it needs a zinc ion, and a common blood protein inhibitor switches it off outside the clot.

A 39-residue peptide from the oral secretion of a venomous lizard. It is released outside the animal's cells, and it switches on one human cell-surface receptor for a gut hormone (the GLP-1 receptor) by binding it. One gene, one chain, no cofactor, no partner protein.

A small ring-shaped chemical made by a sea squirt. It slips into the groove of DNA inside human cells and blocks transcription and repair. Not a protein and not one gene's product; the molecule itself needs no partner.

A mixture of fatty acid esters from fish oil, absorbed from the gut. It changes how the liver handles fat. No single gene makes it, no receptor is named for it, and the effect is on a whole metabolic route rather than on one binding site.

A sugar chain five times longer than the human one, secreted by the skin cells of a long-lived burrowing rodent and left intact because the animal's chain-cutting enzymes are slow. Cells become more sensitive to it, and removing it lets them turn cancerous. It is not one protein: it needs a specific synthase, low cutting activity, and the cell's response to the chain.

A short positively charged peptide based on one that cattle immune cells keep in granules to kill bacteria. It breaks microbial membranes on the skin. One gene, small, no cofactor; it is stored inside the cell that makes it and released on demand, and its target is a microbe rather than a shared animal protein.

A lipid-and-protein extract of cow lung, acting at the air-liquid surface of the lung. It works by lowering surface tension at the air-liquid boundary, a physical effect of the mixture, not by binding a receptor. Many components, several genes, and added lipids are needed for it to work.

A long sulfated sugar chain purified from pig gut lining, not a protein and not the product of one gene. Outside the cell it binds a human blood protein (antithrombin) and makes it trap clotting enzymes much faster. It works only through that partner protein.

A 36-residue disulfide-rich peptide from scorpion venom that binds a receptor on the surface of human brain tumour cells and so marks them. One small folded domain, secreted by the animal, works without partners; it is often joined to a label or a cell.

A protein of a colonial sea squirt that decides whether two colonies fuse or scar. It is found on the inside of the cell membrane and in the nucleus, and the authors suggest it works as a scaffold holding other proteins of the same animal together. One gene, but intracellular, not catalytic, and dependent on partners that only that animal has.
